claim.why_it_matters: A heading at the wrong level (or none) misplaces the clause in the outline that page_workunit, citation and section lookups read, so the clause is attributed to the wrong parent or not found as a section.
claim.note: Heading at the wrong level: the transcription's convention is one '#' per numbering component (7. is '#', 7.1 '##', 6.4.1 '###', 6.4.2.1 '####', 6.4.2.1.1 '#####'); should be '#####'.

verdict.reasoning: Printed page IV-38 (PDF p184) shows '6.4.2.2.2 Definition of Compiler Directing Sentence' as a five-component clause heading. specs/ANSI_COBOL_1985.md line 7691 carries it as '#### 6.4.2.2.2', while the same file's convention gives five-component numbers '#####' (line 7631 '##### 6.4.2.1.1', line 7629 '#### 6.4.2.1', line 7623 '### 6.4.2'). At '####' the heading sits at the level of 6.4.2.1, so an outline reader makes it a sibling of 6.4.2.1 rather than a child of 6.4.2.2. The text is present and correct; the defect is the heading level only. The neighbours have the same shift (6.4.2.2 at '###', 6.4.2.2.1 and 6.4.2.1.2 at '####'), so the subtree is off by one level throughout.
verdict.corrected_description: A wrong-level heading, not a missing one: '6.4.2.2.2 Definition of Compiler Directing Sentence' is transcribed at '####' (md line 7691) and should be '#####' by the file's one-'#'-per-component convention. Its parent 6.4.2.2 (at '###') and siblings 6.4.2.2.1 and 6.4.2.1.2 (at '####') have the same off-by-one shift.
